source.title: FaithUn: Toward Faithful Forgetting in Language Models by Investigating the Interconnectedness of Knowledge
source.authors: Nakyeong Yang; Minsu Kim; Seunghyun Yoon; Joongbo Shin; Kyomin Jung

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened, but the method-to-value layout is recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own unlearning experiments and argues that existing methods can forget target QA items while failing on related paraphrased or interconnected knowledge, refining what successful unlearning should mean. It does not test the specified quantization or fine-tuning recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates unlearning on real-world entity QA. It tests paraphrased questions and reports target-set unlearning stopping at UA≤0.33. It does not apply a relearning attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization, jailbreak, or language-switch attack. Multi-hop and same-answer metrics are reported, but they are not direct tests of the claim versions as worded.
record.test_reason: The paper unlearns real-world entity facts in Gemma-2 2B/9B and Llama-3.2 3B with six baselines plus KLUE. It reports post-unlearning accuracy on paraphrased forget questions (a rephrasing attack, version E) and test-set retention (version A's 'keeps general ability'). It also argues unlearning is superficial because multi-hop knowledge survives and same-answer facts are erased. No relearning, ablation, quantization, jailbreak or language attacks are run.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors define 'superficial unlearning' as failing to erase interconnected (multi-hop) knowledge or erasing unrelated same-answer knowledge. They find existing methods superficial and KLUE better. They also state that all methods handle paraphrases well (UA‡ tracks UA), i.e. rephrasing does not recover the facts.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates unlearning methods on its own real-world entity QA benchmark, with a 5% forget set and early stopping at UA≤0.33. It does not reproduce Who's Harry Potter, the original WMDP evaluation, or the eight-method robustness evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Model, method, forget-set size (1%, 5%, 10%), and MCQA prompt template; the paper reports different outcomes across these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearned models keep answering multi-hop questions that depend on the forgotten fact (e.g. Table 5 case 2: GAret probability 0.5756→0.5757). Appendix C.5 says no method unlearns 3-hop knowledge. The reported MA aggregates forget-side and test-side accuracy, so no forget-side rate is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning a fact leaves downstream multi-hop knowledge that depends on it intact.

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline methods erase unrelated facts that share the forgotten answer ('shortcut unlearning'): SA drops, e.g. Gemma-2 2B GA 37.19 vs 79.63 default.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning suppresses the answer token regardless of context, damaging unrelated same-answer facts.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: No comparison to a model that never learned the target knowledge; no direct recovery attack beyond paraphrased QA and alternate MCQA instructions. Main tables report three-trial averages without error bars. Accuracy on the paraphrase set is not a direct weight-level measure.
record.rows_left_out: Same-answer Accuracy (SA), Multi-hop Accuracy (MA), qualitative probability-shift cases, and other KLUE ablations and hyperparameter results are omitted because they do not directly measure the listed recovery versions. Table 4's Test Accuracy values and default rows are also omitted; the paraphrase UA‡ results for the tested forget-set sizes are retained.

untested.parts: No comparison with a never-trained model. No attacks other than paraphrase and instruction-template changes.
Entirely: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
Entirely: no activation ablation or probing of hidden knowledge.
Jailbreaks, other languages and in-context information are untested. Only paraphrases and five MCQA instruction templates (KLUE only) are tested.
KLUE is a new method but is not tested against relearning, ablation, quantization or jailbreak attacks.

missing.what: Same-answer accuracy (SA) per method and model. This is collateral damage to unrelated knowledge, bearing on A's 'keeps general ability'.
Test accuracy for 1% and 10% forget sets, e.g. GA at 10%: TA 28.02 vs 85.34.
Forget-set UA under the five alternative templates rises to 36–39 from 33.33.
Multi-hop (MA, 2-hop and 3-hop) results; aggregate only, forget side not separable.

record.verdict_notes: The UA≤0.33 values are early-stopping selection criteria, not findings. The paper's main evidence of shallowness, multi-hop survival, is reported only as an aggregate that mixes forget-side and retain-side accuracy, so it cannot be mapped to a recovery rate. The partial/absent threshold for UA‡ was set at about 40% against 33.3% chance.

versions.untested_parts: It does not compare recovery against a model that never learned the knowledge. It tests paraphrases, but not the other simple attacks named in the claim.
No fine-tuning attack on an unlearned model using unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Tests paraphrased questions and alternative MCQA instruction templates only; it does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
KLUE is presented as a method for faithful unlearning, not as a method tested against the recovery attacks in the claim.

relation.reason: Reports unlearning accuracy, retention and paraphrase accuracy for several methods.

tranche.reason: A new benchmark plus the argument that unlearning is superficial on interconnected knowledge, with results on A (retention) and E (paraphrase). T3 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: Real-world entity MCQA with 3 options (chance 33%). UA‡ is paraphrase accuracy. Paraphrase sets are small (664 base QA × 3; the 5% forget set gives about 99 paraphrases, 1% about 20), so cells at 40–44 sit only a few questions above chance. No spread is reported beyond 3-trial averages. Tables 2, 3, 4 and 9 are all readable.

statements.correction: FaithUn: Wikidata facts about famous people, already in the models. 3-option MCQA, chance 33%. Unlearning stopped early at UA≤33%. No retrain/gold reference. Instruction-tuned Gemma-2 2B/9B and Llama-3.2 3B. KLUE on Gemma-2 9B: TA 89.83 vs default 89.87, UA‡ 40.40 vs 91.92. Cite under a real-world-knowledge condition or drop it from this bullet.
statements.problem: The bullet names no FaithUn number. It only cites row G9-KLUE-TA (89.83 vs 89.87, correct). Its conditions don't fit FaithUn: the facts there are real-world knowledge already in the models, not fine-tuned in. The measure has a 33% chance level, there is no retrain or gold model, and the models are Gemma-2 2B/9B and Llama-3.2 3B, not 1–8B Llama.

statements.correction: UA‡ is 29.29–48.14 against defaults of 72.22–91.92. Cells at 40–48: G2 RMU/DPOrej; L3 and G9 GAret/DPOrej/KLUE; GA/DPOrej at 1%; GAret/KLUE at 10%; KLUE template 2. Authors say UA‡ correlates strongly with UA (Sec 5.3).
statements.problem: Numbers match Tables 2–4 and 9. Minor: the 40–48 group is a set of specific cells, not whole methods. GAret and KLUE on Gemma-2 2B are at chance (34.01, 36.70), and GA at 1% forget (44.44) is also in the 40–48 group. Across the 5% main tables, 9 of 17 cells are at 29–39.
